A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PDDLLM framework and core study. All 35 pages of v3 and 42 pages of v4, including appendices, were readable through text extraction and visual inspection. Retained material could be matched across renumbering and relocation.

before.justification: v3 reports original planning experiments across nine environments, numerical baseline comparisons, ablations, and physical robot demonstrations.

after.justification: v4 retains those original experiments and adds quantitative robot outcomes, perception-noise evaluations, parameter sensitivity studies, and alternative-backbone results.

M1.justification: v3 describes interval widths as user-supplied hyperparameters. v4 Section 5.1.4 adds data-dependent initialization using the smallest nonzero feature difference and permits LLM-driven merging and subdivision of intervals. This refines predicate generation within the retained predicate-imagination, action-invention, and LoCA pipeline.

E1.justification: The nine planning environments and three robot platforms are retained. Appendix B.13 adds a distinct evaluation scenario: classifying spatial predicates in real two-cube scenes and under injected perception noise. This extends input-condition coverage without replacing the main planning tasks.

E2.justification: The corresponding planning comparisons retain Expert Design, LLMTAMP, LLMTAMP-FF, LLMTAMP-FR, o1-TAMP, R1-TAMP, and RuleAsMem. The new Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B experiments vary PDDLLM's backbone rather than introduce competing planning methods. Newly cited PSALM-V is not evaluated as a baseline.

E3.justification: v4 adds substantial evaluation protocols: 50 balanced trials per spatial predicate and 5–30% injected noise in B.13; controlled granularity and parallel-prompt sweeps in B.15–B.16; and Qwen3-4B/8B configurations in B.21. The existing planning time budgets are retained; newly specified defaults do not establish that the original experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond v3's task-complexity, time-budget, prompt-style, demonstration-quality, and partition-count analyses, v4 adds perception-noise tests, quantitative granularity sensitivity, prompt-count effects on domain failure and quality, a language-guidance case study, and backbone ablations (B.13, B.15–B.16, B.18, B.21). These address several previously untested robustness questions.

E5.justification: v3 already reports planning success as means and standard errors from three runs. v4 additionally identifies Table 3's predicate-error percentages as three-run averages, reports ten-trial robot outcomes, and discloses five individual token-cost trials. These extend statistical transparency without establishing an increase over previously unspecified run counts.

E6.justification: Tables 1, 2, and 4 retain their numerical results. Table 3 changes stacking missing/redundant percentages from 0.0/12.5 to 4.2/8.3 and adds redundancy in burger cooking and bridge building. New results include robot successes of 9/10, 8/10, 7/10, and 7/10, noise and sensitivity measurements, token-trial values, and Qwen backbone overall success rates of 93.1% and 93.6%.

T1.justification: v4 adds an expressivity argument tying allowable discretization granularity to the smallest nonzero feature difference (5.1.4 and B.15), which v3 does not provide. This is an unproved mathematical bound argument. The existing feature-space definition, planning formulation, and complexity derivation in A.10.2/B.10.2 are retained.

C1.justification: The abstract changes domain construction 'without manual domain initialization' to construction with 'minimal' initialization, and the introduction similarly qualifies the predesign claim. The three central contributions and main performance claims remain. The conclusion still retains the stronger claim of complete domain generation from scratch, so the qualification is only partial.

C2.justification: v4 substantially expands the explanation of missing complex predicates into backtracking, extra feasibility checks, and failures under limited planning budgets (Section 9 and B.17). B.14 adds explicit applicability boundaries concerning structured geometry, stable object properties, deformable materials, precision manipulation, and changing environments. It also adds interpretations of perception tolerance, language-guided refinement, and backbone independence.

D1.justification: v4 specifies the default ten parallel prompts and granularity setting, supplies an action-selection prompt, and documents execution-failure replanning and its stopping conditions (Sections 6, B.7, B.19). These supplement the existing implementation information; hardware, API usage, Pi0 fine-tuning, demonstration collection, and access information are retained.

R1.justification: v4 adds PSALM-V, Kase et al.'s perception-based domain learning, and Kaelbling and Lozano-Perez's hierarchical TAMP work. It expands discussion of environmental feedback and revises how prior methods depend on human feedback and predefined skills. Most other reference changes update metadata or consolidate duplicate citations to the same work.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence remain. v4 locally rewrites method explanations, domain-correction discussion, and limitations; separates future work from the conclusion; and adds reproducibility, ethics, and LLM-use statements. The original appendix becomes Appendix B. These are limited reorganizations rather than a wholesale narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: v4 adds substantial tabular presentation for robot outcomes, noise tests, parameter sweeps, language examples, token trials, and backbone results (Tables 5 and 13–19). Figure 2 revises threshold notation and diagram details, and the predicate-example table changes its displayed categories. ICLR formatting also changes headers and page flow, while the existing performance plots and robot photographs are retained.

improvement.justification: v4 addresses important evidence gaps by quantifying previously illustrated robot deployments and adding systematic tests of perception noise, domain-generation sensitivity, and backbone dependence. Together with operating defaults and clearer applicability limits, these substantially strengthen the paper's empirical support and assessability despite unchanged core benchmark scores. Some new prose overstates reliability: B.16.1 claims consistent generation with five or more prompts, while Table 15 reports 8.3% failures at five and ten. This local inconsistency limits that claim but does not outweigh the gains.
